    21	## When to use image mounts
    22	
    23	Image mounts are appropriate for the following types of use case:
    24	
    25	- Debugging a minimal or hardened image that doesn't include a shell or common
    26	  utilities. You can mount a tool-rich image, such as `busybox`, into the
    27	  running container's namespace and run those tools without changing the
    28	  original image. For a worked example, see
    29	  [Debug with Docker Hardened Images](/dhi/how-to/troubleshoot/).
    30	
    31	- Sharing read-only assets, such as datasets, models, or static content, that
    32	  are distributed as an image and consumed by containers running a different
    33	  image.
    34	
    35	- Keeping application images small by packaging optional tooling in a separate
    36	  image and mounting it only when needed.
    37	
    38	## Mounting over existing data
    39	
    40	If you mount an image into a directory in the container in which files or
    41	directories exist, the pre-existing files are obscured by the mount. This is
    42	similar to if you were to save files into `/mnt` on a Linux host, and then
    43	mounted a USB drive into `/mnt`. The contents of `/mnt` would be obscured by the
    44	contents of the USB drive until the USB drive was unmounted.
    45	
    46	With containers, there's no straightforward way of removing a mount to reveal
    47	the obscured files again. Your best option is to recreate the container without
    48	the mount.
    49	
    50	## Considerations and constraints
    51	
    52	- Image mounts are always read-only. The container can't modify the mounted
    53	  image, and changes aren't persisted anywhere.
    54	
    55	- The source image must already exist in the daemon's image store. Docker
